My understanding of a political platform was one that embraced a broader view which did not contain specific solutions or proposals for the future internal organization of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is something that I plainly described by saying that one ought to distinguish important matters from unimportant matters and contested matters from uncontested matters. Conclusions reached at the meeting were as follows: President Tudjman endorsed the idea and principles, the gist of which was conveyed in Mr. Prlic's speech as well as mine. It was also concluded that at the forthcoming peace conference, we ought to advocate precisely the issues that were touched upon in Mr. Prlic's speech as well as mine. This is something that we did in the subsequent negotiations that took place at the peace conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic was recording the principles of the European Community. Is it your sense that this was to be taken into consideration by Tudjman and all the participants? Does that mean that not just anything could be done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to remind the Trial Chamber of the fact that by that time, the Badinter Arbitration Commission had already expressed its conclusions which were publicised, and according to which Bosnia-Herzegovina was a state of three constituent peoples, and that the treaties of the international community, namely, the UN Charter, the Paris Declaration, and other international instruments, were to be applied by that state. This included the international regulations which had to do with the rights of peoples and ethnic minorities. The Badinter Commission also expressed clear views about the fact that all the entities in Bosnia-Herzegovina had a right to formulate their own administrative structures in the field of justice administration, police, education, and other areas of vital national interests. At the end of the day, a recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or rather, the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the month of April was achieved on a condition that it recognise and accede to these treaties. Therefore, our views expressed at this meeting in Zagreb were based on these very views advanced by an international arbitration commission on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this lengthy answer. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. We're going to move on to another area, and dealing with matters that occur on or about October 17, 1992, that's the general topic area. First document is P 00596.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And with some of these documents, Mr. Buntic, we don't need to dwell on too much; others we will have to, but if you bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: P 00596. We see that these are the rules of procedure of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you would confirm that, correct? You would confirm one that you recognise these as the rules and that these rules were being applied.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the rules of procedure that were passed on the 17th October 1992 at the Presidency session, and it was applied in the work of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now we'll move on to the next document. P 00684, P 00684.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we'll probably have to spend some time on this, not too much I hope, and the Judges may have some questions. This is a decision on amending the statutory decision of the provisional organization of the executive power and administration in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And, very briefly, we see from Article 1 that the HVO has the power to adopt decrees, decisions, dispositions, and conclusions. We have a definition of these instruments, and we see the hierarchy. Still with Article 1, we see that it says that: "The HVO shall also decide by a conclusion when it does not adopt other documents." Then it also says: "In case not suffering delay, the HVO shall adopt enactments falling within the competence of the Presidency of the HZ HB with the understanding that it shall be duty-bound to submit these enactments for consent to the Presidency of the HZ HB at the first session of the Presidency allowing the adoption of such enactments." Then it goes on that: "These enactments indicated in the preceding paragraph," the one I just read, that is, "shall be in force as of the day of their adoption ..." Now, it would appear that on 17 October 1992, as a result of Article 1, the powers of the HVO, this temporary executive authority, their powers were to some extent increased. Would you not agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was adopted, and a similar one was adopted by the parliament of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A decision was made to provide for a situation in which the parliament could no longer be convened, and its powers were transferred on to the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The parliamentary body could not be convened during the war, and its authorities were delegated to a smaller and more operational body. The purpose of the decision which was adopted on the 17th of October at the Presidency session, the Presidency of the HZ HB, was if not the same then at least similar, and the goal was more or less identical. The authorities of the larger and bulkier, so to speak, body were delegated to a smaller body, and the Presidency by this decision authorised the HVO to make decisions in emergencies and also to adopt regulations that would otherwise fall within the purview of the Presidency. At the moment when this statistician was adopted, we did not think that the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna would never be convened again. The decision was adopted in order to provide for the adoption of the regulations between the two Presidency sessions. That was the meaning of this decision, and then any regulations that would have been adopted in such a way in emergency would be submitted for a ratification to the Presidency. Then if the Presidency approved them they would remain in effect; and if the Presidency failed to approve them, then they would no longer be implemented and they would no longer be in effect as of the date when the Presidency adopted a decision to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unless there are any questions, I will be moving on, Your Honours. 1D 0073. And, again, we can go through some of these documents rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see this is 17 October 1992. This is a decree on the establishment of a department of the public prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during the war -- during war or the imminent threat of war. And from Article 1, we see that this is an affiliate department. Now, this is what you were speaking about yesterday, some creative measures had to be taken such as establishing affiliate or branch departments or offices, and this is an example of it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection to the leading question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was based -- it was based in part on the testimony of the gentleman from yesterday. I can understand the Prosecution wanting to eat up my time, but that was the purpose of the narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not trying to eat up counsel's time, Mr. President, but I do think that there is something that the witness can contribute in introducing the document as opposed to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could comment very briefly on this document, keeping in mind the comments that you gave us yesterday, your rather lengthy narrative on this topic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to refer to my testimony provided yesterday, during which I explained the reasons for which this decree was adopted and the reasons preceding the establishment of the department of the public prosecutor's office in Mostar. This is not about the establishment of a body of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It is just one department of the republican body, which is clearly stated under Article 1 of this decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 00074.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a decree on the implementation of the Law on Public Order and Order of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during war or the imminent threat of war. And, here, I just want to focus a little bit on Article 1. It says: "The Law on Public Law and Order of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," it goes on, "shall be applicable on the territory of the Croatian Community." And then under Article 2, we see some amendments. If you could very briefly tell us, these amendments, what do they reflect, just very quickly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It arises from this decree that the republican law of Bosnia-Herzegovina is being adopted, the law that regulates this matter. And the law is being adopted in its totality, save for in the part in which Yugoslav dinars are being translated into Croatian dinars. The rest remains in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's look at 1D 00075.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You are saying, Mr. Buntic, that this decree says that, as it stands, the law for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is being adopted. Now, if I look at this text here, I find - I hope I'm not mistaken - Article 4 where it says: "The Presidency of HZ HB appoints the deputies to the republican public prosecutor's office." Article 4. Am I in the wrong document because that probably is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let my words become chocolate, as we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we can go back to 1D 00073.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No. It's not necessary because this is not claimed to be taking over the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And the purpose, Your Honours, is to show that the laws themselves, the substantive part, is the same except for the monetary values that are being amended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can see that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go on to the next document, 1D 00075.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The same would apply for this particular decree; that is, without leading you too much, that it is the same law that is being adopted with the exception that there's some amendments in Article 2 dealing with monetary fines that will be reflected in dinars. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just another example showing that all the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina were adopted with some necessary interventions that had to be implemented in order for the laws to be applied in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can we say the same thing for 1D 00076, 1D 00076, which is the decree on the change of the Republic of BiH Law on Public Gathering in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that was said about the previous documents applies to this one, and everything that I provided as answers to your previous questions may be an answer to this question as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next document, which is 1D 00087.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see that here just very quickly, just so the Chamber can get an idea, this is a decision to appoint the district military prosecutor in Mostar and a deputy district military prosecutor. And, so, do you recall whether these individuals actually served at some point or another as a result of this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision to appoint the district military prosecutor and the deputy district military prosecutor, which was adopted on the 17th of October, 1992. If the names of these persons are correct, they were, indeed, appointed. Mladen Jurisic was appointed to the post of district military prosecutor, and Ekrem Insanic and Mario Bogdanovic were appointed to the posts of deputy district military prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Are all three of them Croats?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you content yourself with a partial answer, because you have also asked whether these persons did actually take up and exercise their function .

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did they actually function once they had been nominated? Did they take office and act the role that they were assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the appointment, they did take their roles. They worked in their respective posts, but they could not assume their posts immediately because there were no premises of the district military court, i.e., there was no building where they could work. That's why they could not embark on their work immediately after being appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you have an idea, can you tell the Bench when they did actually start, when the infrastructure was sufficient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was sometime in spring 1993. It was only then that the premises were re-appointed. They started working sometime in March or April 1993. It's very similar to the situation with this Tribunal. It certainly didn't start working on the day when it was established, and the same goes for the Prosecution, I believe. I believe that it took some time for the Prosecutor's office to become fully operational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And that would be time after March or April? They start in March or April, but then until they are functional some more time elapses? Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only in March or April they moved into the offices in a building of the school of law in Mostar. That's when they were given premises where they could work. And you, of course, know that it takes some time for any decisions to be made and especially when it comes to judiciary. This was just the beginning. This was just the moment when the conditions were put in place to allow them to start working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I absolutely understand that. And can you give some precision or some indication on how long it took from the taking of office in the physical sense until they had become operative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that they become -- they became operational sometime in summer or autumn 1993, but I say that it was sooner in the summer than in the autumn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And very quickly on the names, are they all Croats that were being appointed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic and Mr. Bogdanovic are Croats, and Mr. Insanic is a Muslim, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to go through about three or four other documents very quickly. These are just decisions on appointments, if you could confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next document is 1D 00088.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we see that this is a decision to appoint -- to elect a president of the high court in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that this decision was indeed adopted on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then 1D 00081.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a decision that relieves the judge of the lower court in Capljina, because we'll see that he's going to be going to another duty. So can you confirm this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm this decision, and I also confirm that Mr. Katic was relieved of his duty as judge and was appointed as prosecutor by another decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have a decision where four judges were appointed to the district military court, dated again 17 October 1992. Can you confirm that this decision was passed; and to follow-up on some of the questions from Judge Trechsel, did they actually take their post at some point and begin to work, as you've indicated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that is said about the decision concerning military prosecutors applies to the military court as well. It is about the same buildings which was reappointed for that person and it only happened in spring 1993, which means that they started working only then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 00083.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here, we have a decision to appoint Kresimir Zubak, who was a lawyer from Doboj and, as I understand it, was also a judge there at some point. He's appointed as vice-president of the Croatian Community. Can you confirm this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that this decision was adopted at the Presidency session on the 17th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go on to P 00590, P 00590.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I would ask you to kindly read the title of the decree because, as I understand it, it may need to be corrected from the English title that we have here. This is from the Official Gazette. So could you please tell us what -- read the title to this decree.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decree on district military prosecutor's offices in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in times of war or the immediate threat of war. Article 3: "The district military prosecutor's office shall prosecutor perpetrators of criminal acts that fall within the jurisdiction of district military courts and are subject to prosecution ex officio. Accordingly, it shall ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. No, that's fine. Just so we know, was this decree actually applied to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This decree was applied, as I already told you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if there are no questions from the Court and the Judges, I'll move on. All right. P 00594.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a decree on the establishment of a department of the public prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, two questions: One, did this decree come into effect; and secondly, and more importantly, what exactly did this department of the prosecution's office do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke yesterday about the reasons behind the establishment of the republican prosecutor's office, i.e., the council of the republican prosecutor's office in Mostar. This was because the public prosecutor of Bosnia and Herzegovina could not exercise his authorities in any territory outside of Sarajevo. It was physically impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did this decree actually go into effect?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decree did go into effect, and it was applied for as long as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And attached to this particular exhibit, we see two other decrees: One on the implementation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I already would like to ask in a way the expression of the affiliate department. Here, we see: "During war or the imminent threat of war, an affiliate department of the republican public prosecutor's office," et cetera, "shall be established ..." I wonder if, under this affiliate, it would like to suggest that it is in addition to other departments which have been working already, or does it mean some special kind of status, to speak about affiliation? I'm not quite sure that that in the original B/C/S, the "uredbu," et cetera, if this affiliate is included or not. Probably Mr. Buntic may tell us what the affiliate department would have meant to mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our judicial practice or in our judiciary practice, there always existed court branch offices and prosecutor's branch offices. For example, the municipal court in Mostar had its branch offices or affiliated offices in Citluk and Nevesinje in other municipalities there, and there were days when judges worked in these affiliated departments. Just like the department in Citluk which was affiliated with the court in Mostar was never an independent court. It was just a department of the municipal court in Mostar. The same applied to the municipality of Nevesinje. These two departments or branch offices did not have the status of a legal subject. They were just parts of the republican prosecutor's office if we are talking about the prosecutor's office, or the republican courts if we're talking about the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Buntic, for this explanation. My problem is that in the title of the decree itself, it says: "Decree on the establishment of a department of the public prosecutor's office ..." Whereas, in Article 1, it says: "During the war," et cetera, "an affiliate department of the republican public prosecutor's office," et cetera, "shall be established ..." Now, it is why I asked the question what the affiliate means, because in the title of the whole decree, we do not have this affiliate, but we do have it in Article 1. So it might be not a very important question, frankly, but I just wanted to clarify if there is any difference between the two expressions as they are figuring in the major title and in Article 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure if the translation of the Croatian version is correct. In Article 1, there appears the word "izmjesteno" which does not exist in the heading, which was translated in English, I don't know how. But what it means is that it is outside of the head office. The republican courts and prosecutor offices normally had their head office; whereas, this term practically means that it is a branch office, it is not housed in the main seat of a court of law. I don't know if that's what you are referring to. It's relocated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you referred here to the problem of translation. What you meant in Article 1 is that it's devolved or delocated because of the circumstances of war. Is that what you meant, that it's not affiliated, it's devolved? A prosecutor who has been relocated, as it were, because circumstances dictate that he should be elsewhere than where he should normally be, that's why you used this term delocated -- relocated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, relocated. I believe that would be the right term. That it is relocated; that would be the appropriate term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I have another question. I'm somewhat surprised or I wonder why here the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna nominates or creates an office for the public prosecutor of Bosnia and Herzegovina; that is, one entity for another entity. How is this legally possible? I see you smile.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my only answer would be the question: Who else could have done it? There was nobody else; nobody else could have done that. I'm going back again to what I said yesterday. The same thing happened elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The relocated departments were established in Bihac, Tuzla, and Zenica as well, because the republican prosecutor could not reach those areas. Had the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina even passed a decision, there was no way for them to forward it to us in Mostar. There was no other practical solution, and we had to find one. We kept highlighting, however, that this would remain in force while there was a war on, while there was a state of an imminent threat of war. We were not able to reach Sarajevo, nor were we able to wait for the decisions of the Presidency. We had to find functionable solutions and models. We had no use for any other ones that didn't work. They had to be workable. We were faced with problems which we had to solve and solve them in a way that was workable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can understand that, but then why not a department of the public prosecutor's office of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? Why give it a name of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Because I suppose that this prosecutor's office could not function outside of Herceg-Bosna either. Why attach to it the Bosnia and Herzegovina label?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was always our intention to highlight that this was a prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that it was only his deputies that were relocated to that area who worked within a relocated department; in this particular instance, it was in Mostar. We wanted to emphasize the fact that the structure belonged to Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the republican prosecutor's office. The situation involving courts was similar. When we will be referring to the Supreme Court, the reasons behind that particular solution were similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered my question. I think Mr. Karnavas is getting impatient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just one moment. Witness, I'd just like to go back to the time of Yugoslavia, when there was a prosecutor. Was there a prosecutor in Mostar in the days of the former Yugoslavia? In the days of the federal republic, was there a prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, there existed the municipal prosecutor's office in Mostar, that is to say, the prosecutor in the first instance; and the district public prosecutor's office, that's to say, the prosecution in the second instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. When the JNA left, the Serbs left, I assume that the prosecutor was Serbian so he had to leave; or was he Croat or Muslim? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember specifically all the names from that period, but I do know that most of the members of the prosecutor's office in Mostar were Serbs; whereas, in the courts, there was a presence of Serbs that was in proportion larger to their share in the ethnic make-up. We had cases of Serb judges who remained there throughout the war in their capacities as judges or prosecutors, and were never removed from those positions by the HVO. I also said yesterday that most of them, most of the Bosniaks, that's to say, Muslims, who were members of the prosecutor's office or judges, remained in their positions. None of them were removed or demoted. I believe some of them even advanced in their professions, and there is among the documents here a decision which can confirm this, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised, did they have the time to appoint a prosecutor in Mostar or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no. It was at that point in time precisely that problems emerged and that an all-out war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the referendum for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was held; in other words, as soon as the Bosniaks and Croats voted in favour of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbs at their own referendum voted for the Republika Srpska, war activities escalated and Sarajevo became encircled. From that point on, Sarajevo could not be reached, and we're not talking only about the courts. We're talking about the parliament, the government, the Presidency. The Serbs had by that time already abandoned all these structures: Parliament, Presidency, and government. The Bosniaks and Croats kept these structures alive until such time as they were able to meet again. However, as soon as this situation emerged and the war activities broke out, it was impossible -- it became impossible for the government, the Presidency, and the parliament to meet regularly. We were forced to find a solution to make decisions in the absence of those organs. Even where these organs were able to make decisions, it was impossible to physically forward them to Mostar. I don't know if I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. And that's perhaps why, in Article 3, you required that the prosecutor should be a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This definition was taken over from the earlier law. There's nothing novel about that. We're not asking or we're not making a requirement for that person to be a resident of the HZ HB or to in any way be present in the HZ HB; merely that he has to be a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Attached to this particular document, that is, P 00594, we also see a decree on the implementation of the Law on Public Order; and, again, there's also an implementation on the Law on Road Traffic and Safety. And I take it your previous concerning the changes applied to these two decrees? There's no need to dwell on them. Just if you could confirm that, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that. We've already discussed it. These were merely amendments with the purpose of translating Yu dinars into Croatian dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, this is 17 October 1992. This is a decree on district military courts in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in a state of war or an imminent threat of war; and, here, we can see in Article 2 -- or Article 1 that were establishing -- Article 2, I'm sorry: "When performing their functions, district military courts shall act independently and shall administer justice on the basis of the Constitution and the law." Again, this is -- based on your previous answers, this was a necessary decree because of the conditions; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday and today, we discussed the reasons behind these decrees. This decree has to do with district military courts. It was applied in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It was first harmonized in consultation with the deputy minister of justice of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is also something I referred to today. This type of regulation was passed elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the effect that in the territories under the control of the BH army, district military courts and district military prosecutor's offices were set up almost in the same way as had been done in the HZ HB and the territory it covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said when you met with this minister, who again was the ethnicity and what was his ethnicity or national make-up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy minister of justice of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was Jusuf Halilagic. As I've already said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we met in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was his national make-up? These may not seem very consequential to outsiders; but for this case, trust me, every question I ask is pretty important. So, was he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for not answering right away. Jusuf Halilagic was a Muslim or a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, staying with this document, very briefly go to Article 5 (b). I just want to see if maybe you can help us with this a little bit, a comment: "The Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or in cases where communications have been disrupted, the relocated Chamber of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which has itself -- which has its seat in Mostar, shall hear appeals against the decisions of the district military courts, in such cases are mentioned in Article 18, paragraph 2." Now, I take it from -- this would tie-in with your answers yesterday where you indicated that a chamber of the Supreme Court was established because Sarajevo was under siege, basically. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by the answer that I believe I already gave to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Article 5(b), in fact, recognises that the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina is competent unless communications with Sarajevo are disrupted, but the natural Supreme Court remains that of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what seems to be written in Article 5(b).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is best to read it out, and then you -- we can see how it is translated into English. Article 5(b): "The Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or in cases where communications have been disrupted, the relocated Chamber of the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which has its seat in Mostar, shall hear appeals against the decisions of district military courts, if such cases are mentioned in Article 18, paragraph 2." In other words, what this article expressly states is that the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina has the jurisdiction to hear appeals, and where the Supreme Court is unable to hear such cases because communications have been disrupted, and there were such cases documented at the time, the relocated Chamber of that court in Mostar will -- would hear these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 500 -- I mean, P 00589, P 00589.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here, we see the actual decree on establishing an office of the Supreme Court on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in wartime or when there is an imminent threat of war. And just as you've explained, we see Article 1. It talks about: "A relocated office of the Supreme Court ... is to be established ..." Article 2 talks about seven judges to be appointed. And we look at Article 3, which indicates that the office shall be responsible for carrying out functions cited in Articles 39 of the Law on Regular Courts, and it refers to the Official Gazette of Bosnia -- of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that's what you were talking about. This decree establishes the relocated office that we've been speaking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. While we were referring to the relocated department of the public prosecutor's office, I said that everything that applied to the relocated office of the republican prosecutor also applied to the relocated Chamber of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know if there's any need for me to give any further explanation. I believe that the regulations were quite similar, and that we've already discussed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't mean to rush you, Mr. Buntic. It's just that time is of -- time is my enemy in this courtroom at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a decision to appoint the deputy head of the department of justice. This is another example of an appointment being made. Do you recall whether this individual actually took his position based on this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is an appointment of Karlo Sesar, who was an attorney-at-law from Mostar, to the post of deputy head of the justice department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 01979, 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is dated 10 August 1993. It's a list of HZ HB HVO acts, and it says: "Approval requested." Without going through the document itself in any detail, could you please describe to us in one sentence what this document reflects.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the HVO, Mr. Jadranko Prlic, informs the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna through this letter of all the enactments passed by the HVO which fell under the competence of the Presidency. I will go back to what I said earlier. On the 17th of October, 1992, the Presidency passed a decision authorising the HVO to pass regulations from the purview of the Presidency where the situation dictated that. This is a list of the enactments passed by the HVO, which the HVO president submits to the president of the HZ HB for approval. In other words, these were the enactments passed on the basis of the decision of the 17th of October, 1992, and were forwarded for approval to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And that ties in with your previous answer, as you told us when there was an amendment to the statutory decision; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the 17th of October, 1992, amendment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the next document is 1D 02545, 1D 02545, dated -- it's 46, I'm told. So it's 1D 02546.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is an Article from Slobodna Dalmacija, 28 October 1992, and we can see that your name -- you're being quoted, the head of the department of justice. I want to read a couple of parts and then have you comment very quickly. You say in the second paragraph -- or it's said, it's reported: "To begin with, he recalled that the founding enactment of November 1991 defined the HZ of Herceg-Bosna as a cultural, economic, and regional entity of the Croatian people and other peoples who live in the territory. Mr. Buntic explained in more detail that the goal of its foundation was also its development into a constitutional unit of the Croatian people in BH. "The goal, according to Buntic, was grounded in three vital facts: First, the Constitution of BH defined that state as a community of three peoples; furthermore, nowhere anywhere in the world is there a multi-ethnic community as a unitary state; and, third, the EC Commission for BH proceeding from the fact that BH is a compound state of three constituent peoples put forward the concept of a new Constitution in this respect, and so it was directly on such constitutional principles that BH also received international recognition." Mr. Buntic, was this the position that you held then, as is reflected in this article dated 28 October 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that this is my statement. It was accurately conveyed here. The only thing where I disagree with this article is that the journalist styled me as a minister, and I was not a minister. I was a head of the justice department. Everything else, however, is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we were to go back to the previous document that we saw the transcript, that is, the presidential transcript of September, are these more or less the same?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just comment on the last thing you have said, Mr. Buntic. You made a case, and we've heard this before, in the difference between and head of department. Is there a legal basis for such a difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is, and the difference is significant. It's not a minor difference. The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was not a state, nor did it ever wanted to be one. What is emphasized in this statement of mine which was published by a newspaper is that throughout the existence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, its primary goal was to defend the territory from aggression, and it succeeded in that. Just a moment. The second goal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I hear that, and I've heard it before. I know that ideology. But I'm a bit depressed now because it seems that I come from a non-state, because the state where I come from - Switzerland, it's no secret - has only departments and the heads of departments are called head of department. Does that mean that Switzerland is not a state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that the comparison is fair. Judging by what I know about the Swiss constitution, it contains confederal elements, so the Swiss model is not purely a federal model. We may agree to disagree. I preceded my words by saying that this is what I know. In this particular case, I adhere by my words, and that is that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna never wanted to become an independent state. Its primary goal was to organize defence, the defence of its own territory; and the secondary goal was to establish a constituent unit of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina in that area. That goal was never a hidden agenda. You must see that. I promoted it in public. I always promoted that goal during international negotiations, during the talks that were transcribed. And you can see here that I consistently adhered to what was transcribed and stated at several places. There were no aberrations, there were no hidden agendas, there were no different policies, and at different times; the goals were always the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not addressing the issue behind it, only the terminology. Am I correct in understanding you as saying: We choose on purpose the term "department" rather than "ministry" to demonstrate that Herceg-Bosna was not supposed to be regarded as a state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It did not have a legal foundation for that. It didn't -- it wasn't a state. It did not have a constitution. It did not have any legal foundation to call me or anybody else who was the head of any department at the time a minister. Those were not ministries. Those were just these departments. If you have a ministry, then its head is a minister; if you have departments, then its head is only the head of that department. This was a regional community of municipalities which was not a state. It did not have ministers; therefore, it could not have ministers as such. I personally was not very pleased when I was called minister. Some other people were pleased. But I myself did not like being called minister. And as I said here, the journalist wanted to flatter me and portray me as something else to the general public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me for stopping you, but I do it for Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I have a follow-up question on this because if we fast-forward a little bit to the creation of the -- or the establishment, I should say, of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, there we do see that ministries as opposed to heads of departments are called for. Now, can you explain that, that transition from department to ministry; that's number one. And number two, should the Trial Chamber from the fact that now we have ministries as opposed to departments, that now the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna is a state within a state?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that certain parallels should be drawn here as well between what had existed up to then in Yugoslavia and what was happening on the international scene. When the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was being constituted, the international community had offered the Owen-Stoltenberg peace plan which implied a confederation of three constituent units in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was to be at the confederal model of the organization of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In practical terms, this would mean that there would be a contract between three independent states, a confederal state, the federal level would have only very minor parts of state authorities and all the other competencies and authorities would remain with the constituent units. The foundation for the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was the stage reached in the peace talks within the peace conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina. The plan that was offered was partially adopted. Its constitutional principles were adopted, and the main sticking points were some minor territorial issues. The Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna based its foundation in the Owen-Stoltenberg plan. It considered this plan a favourable solution for Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They deemed the plan acceptable, and they acted or reacted by establishing the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. If we're talking about a confederation, then we are talking about an alliance of sovereign states; and it is only logical that in such a state, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna would have been a state with its ministry. And this would have been the case if the Owen-Stoltenberg plan had taken off the ground. The only ministries that would have been at the federal level were the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We need to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have exactly 45 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I have one last question regarding the document that we were discussing. But before I do that, I just want to pick up on your last answer, because you described to us basically your understanding of the Owen-Stoltenberg, what it envisaged; that is, three republics. If you could in one sentence, just tell us, when you compare the Owen-Stoltenberg plan and what ultimately emerged at Dayton under the Dayton Peace Accords where you have two entities - the federation which came about from the Washington Agreement and the Republika Srpska - are there any major differences between those two peace plans?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, there are major differences. Again, I can only give you my opinion, nothing else. What happened in Dayton is not what I consider a good solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would have never personally accepted that solution, and I still claim that Vance-Owen Plan and the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan were much better solutions for Bosnia and Herzegovina. And as may be seen from all of my public appearances and propositions, I believe it was a clear constitutional foundation, a foundation in international documents for both the implementation of Owen-Stoltenberg and Vance-Owen plans. The solution as it was at the moment and was adopted for Bosnia and Herzegovina is what I consider --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm having problems. I'm not aware of any such similar model in the world. I don't know of any one state that consists of three constituent peoples which has been organized in the way Bosnia and Herzegovina has been organized. For one people to be recognised the rights that have been denied to the other two peoples, that would be the gist of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Setting aside that aspect, when it comes to the relationship between the entities and the state in the Dayton Peace Accords versus, say, the relationship between the republics and the state and the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, that is, the powers that were given to the republics, you know, and those that were kept by the state in the one plan and again the powers given to the entities and those that were kept by the state; are there any major differences there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the differences between the Dayton and the Washington Agreements, then we're talking about two entities; and if we're talking about two entities, I could say that the Serbian entity has kept the rights that were envisaged by the Owen --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I'm trying to draw a parallel between the powers that the republics would have had in the Owen-Stoltenberg and the state. You said the state would have certain powers. The rest would be allocated to the republics. Now I'm asking you to look at the Dayton. Never mind that the Croats were bundled together with the Muslims as a result of the Washington Agreement to form the Federation. Setting aside that, when you look at what was envisaged initially and what was being implemented initially at Dayton, the powers given to the entities and those that were kept by the state, are there similarities or differences between the two peace plans?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I have understood you properly, but I already started answering you. When it comes to the entities, the powers are very similar. The Owen-Stoltenberg implied two entities, and the other agreements implied three entities --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The other way around.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But according to Owen-Stoltenberg, there were three entities; and according to the Washington and Dayton Accords, there are two entities. And I already started talking in that sense and answering you in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies for framing the question inartfully, but that's basically what I wanted to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention. Then, just one last point with respect to this last document, which was 1D 02545, we can see in the very last paragraph of your -- of the interview where you're attributed to having said: "The department head, Buntic, pointed out the need for representatives of the Muslim people to take on their share of responsibility in those provisional authorities. According to him, during the recent visit to Mostar by President Alija Izetbegovic, accord was reached on a proposal that the Muslims in Mostar should participate in the authorities, administrative organs, and public activities in a ratio of 50/50; and at the level of the constituent units, namely, HZ of Herceg-Bosna, they should participate with 35 per cent." Could you please explain that to us. I don't recall having much testimony in this courtroom in the last two and a half years about Alija Izetbegovic being in Mostar. We briefly touched on it, but maybe you could elaborate a little bit before we go on to the next segment.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was obtained from the then-leadership of the SDA for the region of Herzegovina about this visit by Mr. Izetbegovic. People that I contacted informed me that some agreements were reached, and that the HDZ and the SDA were participating in the power in the ratio of 50/50 in Mostar, and in Herzegovina the ratio would be 35 per cent. I'm giving you this on the basis of the information that I received from the then-leadership of the SDA for Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., based on my conversation with Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. This deals primarily with the judiciary. So we'll first start off with P 01264, P 01264.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I just want to focus your attention on page 3 in the English version where it says: "Formal oath." We can see from this document that this is the 21st Session of the Croatian Defence Council meeting on 22 January 1993, and all I want to do is focus your attention where it says "formal oath."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at item 2 on page 2, Your Honours, at the bottom, we can see that this is the oath that would be given to judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It says, and I quote: "I pledge that I will abide by the Constitution, the law, and other existing regulations, and through conscientious work, I will protect the interests and the state system of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of BH, and that I will perform my duty and task conscientiously." Now, no doubt, the judges are asking themselves why the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna first, and then the Republic of BH. And can we draw any conclusions from that, that would be contrary to this, to any allegiance to the state, that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see here that this statement was adopted at the meeting on 22nd January 1993; thus, we are already in 1993. And today, as I'm reading this statement, I can see that some things may be changed, that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina could precede the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I'm talking about the order of the words. As for the rest of the statement by which the judges are asked to abide by constitutions and laws of both the Republic of Croatia -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I believe that the rest of this statement is correct, this oath. The only thing, as I've said, it could be the inversion of places between the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. But what is implied here is that the constitutionality of both should be respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: An additional question on this text of the oath. Is "Bog," God, a word that refers equally to the Judeo-Christian God, and for Mohammed to Allah; or is it to be understood as a Catholic-Christian's god. And attached to the question, an atheist judge, is that conceivable and could he have sworn otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was discussed. The issue was discussed, and I know that Bosniaks who took the oath. I had taken with them before the ceremony; and for them, it was Allah. There were no problems with that. The overall atmosphere was one of understanding and respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the former Yugoslavia in the federal republic, would judges take an oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They did take an oath. The wording was similar to the wording of this oath. But when the state is mentioned here, the oath implied that they were to uphold the state of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. And this did not imply just the state that it was but its ideology, the socialist and communist ideology that were contained in the title of the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in that particular oath, was any reference made to God, or was this something that was added later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no reference of that sort in the previous statement. God was not mentioned. The former regime was atheist, and there was a ban on mentioning God or indicating God in any shape or form. And if the oath had been worded in that way, it would have been contrary to the then-constitution of the socialist and communist Yugoslavia, as existed at the time. An oath of this type would have been incriminated, and whoever wanted -- might have wanted to push that would certainly have been prosecuted. By including this word, a distinction was being made between the new regime and the former regime during which God could not be mentioned for over 40 years in any shape or form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Buntic. Now we're going to move rather quickly on some documents, and others I will have you comment more on them. So I just need a confirmation on a couple of documents to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These are minutes of the 4th Session of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, 22 September 1992. We see that your name is there, having participated. And, of course, if we go to page 4 in the English text, I don't know exactly on what page it's yours, but we see that you do mention or you give an explanation on the judicial system and propose the election of judges to the district and military courts. Can you confirm that at that session, you provided these explanations? We will get to the laws. I just need the confirmation for the purposes of this document.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't just say yes. I believe that this calls for an explanation. If you look at the date of this session, we can see that this was on the 22nd of September, 1992; and that in this particular case, proposals were tabled based on the previously adopted decree, a decree that was adopted on the 3rd of July, which was never adopted in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as we know, and it was never published. These proposals were tabled based on that decree that was never adopted and applied, and we have already spoken about that before this Trial Chamber. And we said that the decree that was, in fact, implemented was passed on the 17th of October, 1992. In other words, these were proposals with the caveat that they were tabled based on a decree that was never applied. And that's why these proposals were never adopted, but, rather, the proposals that were adopted were those that were adopted after the 17th October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, unless there are any questions from the Bench, I'll move on to the next document, which is P 00543.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is from minutes of the 5th Session, 29 September 1992. Again, we see that you're named as having been present; and, again, I just need just a confirmation, sir, because we will get to some of the details later on. If we look on page 8 in the English version, we see that you report that: "The department works in a very difficult condition -- or works in difficult conditions (no telephone, machine workshop is in the same building, no police security)." And then you propose that the Presidency meet more often and that the Presidency separate the jurisdiction of the HVO from that of the Presidency. Now, perhaps you would comment on this because this might be of some importance. We can see that you're having difficult conditions; but the latter part, the separation between Presidency and the HVO and your urging the Presidency to meet more often.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already yesterday, we spoke at great length about some ambiguities with regard to the separation between the powers of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the executive body. I believe that we elaborated that topic yesterday. We spoke about the powers that were concentrated in one person who united several functions, and he could not discharge all of them. That's why regulations had to be adopted in order to separate all these powers and authorities. That is one thing. Here, it is pointed for the need for the Presidency to meet more often because such meetings - and we already said that the authorities that were handed over to the HVO - that these were valid between the Presidency sessions which called for decisions to be made urgently. And we know that after the session which took place on the 17th of October, no single Presidency session was ever held again; and that at the Presidency sessions - and I don't know whether it has been reflected on all the records - but I remember that at many sessions of the HVO, this need was pointed out. It is true that this was discussed, and I believe that the record correctly reflects my discussion. I was at that meeting, and I remember my words very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now we go on to the next document, which is P 00559.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And these are the minutes from the 6th Session, 7 October 1992; and here's where you will need to give us some explanations. If you could be as brief as you can, unless of course the Trial Chamber asks the question and then you can go ahead, be as expansive as you want. But in looking at item 3, this is on page 3 of the English version, and I'm going to be looking at page 3 and page 4. Here, it says that you proposed two versions of a decree on temporary establishment of courts and proceedings before courts in the area of HZ HB. Now, you already talked earlier about a draft that was never published and never implemented. When we look at what you -- these minutes, we see that there is version 1 and version 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, of course, I was referring to the earlier document for Your Honours' attention, which was P 09552, when I said that he had indicated that it was drafted but never actually implemented or published.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which of the two versions was implemented ultimately that is reflected in this, in these minutes - can you just answer that question first - version one or version two?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minutes clearly show that the department of justice and general administration drafted two versions. The argumentation in favour of version one was presented here. It was stated that by adopting version one, one would avoid the setting up of a dual justice administration system, one would guarantee the legality of the decisions rendered by it. It allowed for the possibility to abolish the decisions challenging jurisdiction. It was also said that this version was discussed with representatives of Bosniaks or Muslims, or rather, the minister of justice of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Ultimately, version one was adopted and implemented at the meeting of 17 October 1992 of the HVO HZ HB. Version two provided for the establishment of a separate and autonomous system. We said that this was adopted at the meeting of the 3rd of July and had never been applied simply because it had never been published in the Official Gazette of the HZ HB. This was something we discussed earlier on reference to some documents, and here you can find an explanation of why that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, unless there are any questions -- sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will allow Judge Trechsel to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe I'm again mistaken in the document; but the last-but-three lines from the paragraph of 4, I read: "Since that is not possible due to the above reasons, the draft decree (version two) was unanimously agreed..." And you have just said, Mr. Buntic, that the decision had been for version number one. So I find it difficult not to see a certain contradiction, but probably I have something wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such an interpretation is possible, too; however, what I'm talking about is what the Presidency of the HZ HB decided upon. At the 17th of October, 1992, meeting, as you can clearly see, version one was adopted on the organization and run of the justice administration system: The decisions on setting up the department of the Supreme Court of the Republic of BH, the department of the republican prosecutor's office, the department of the republican misdemeanours court. In other words, the justice administration system of the BH remained intact, and district courts were set up based on the same principles and the practice employed by the Bosniaks. I'm talking about what was officially carried, publicised, and implemented in our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honour, in saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, do you allow for the possibility that perhaps the minutes are wrong; in other words, that there it was recorded wrong? Because if you look at the rest of the sentence, and then if you could look at the Croatian version with the ERN number 0403995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could assist us here, I can point to the -- Mr. Usher, if you could be so kind to assist. And, of course, this is a follow-up from Judge Trechsel's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Evidently the text in brackets, "version two," deviates and departs from the full tenure and meaning of the discussions at the meetings, as well as from the explanations and conclusions provided. In my view, the text in brackets, namely, the word "two" was a mistake. It should instead read "one." This is what follows from the text as it stands. It follows that the word "two" is an error. The text in its entirety indicates that version one was adopted, because the text then says: "The Presidency of the HZ HB should be personally acquainted with version one." In other words, the Presidency should become familiarized with version one, not two. In my view, this is a typographical error in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it - again, a follow-up question from Judge Trechsel's question - if we were to look at the actual implementing instruments and compare them with the two versions, what was actually implemented ultimately would be version one versus version two. That's the conclusion that could be drawn by doing such a comparison?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the document subsequently issued by the Presidency, it becomes obvious that version one was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unless there are any questions, we go on to the next document, 1D 02001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is - again, we're going to move rather quickly - 9 October 1992. There are proposals for elections, and I just want to -- we see your name at the bottom. I want to focus your attention to the last paragraph. It says: "The Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina has already appointed the following Muslim members of the District Military Court in Mostar," and then we see three names. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that this is my letter sent to the municipal board of the Mostar Party of Democratic Action, to the president personally, wherein I inform the president of the Mostar SDA that the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had in the meantime appointed the three judges listed therein. We can clearly see that all the three judges were of Bosniak ethnicity, and this letter asks the SDA to provide their nominations for the president of the misdemeanour court in Mostar, for the president of the lower court in Mostar as it was called at the time, and their nominee for the president of the district military court in Mostar. The nominees were, in fact, sent to me and forwarded to the department for defence in order for these appointments to take effect. In addition to the three judges, therefore, which were nominated by the Presidency for judges of the high court in Mostar, Mr. Memic was subsequently appointed; in other words, there were four Bosniaks and four Croats in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 00113, 1D 00113.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a decree, it's on the Law on Civil Procedure, and, of course, we saw similar such decrees dealing with -- I don't know if it was criminal or criminal procedure. But if we look at again where this decree adopts what is already in existence with the change of the amounts quoted in dinars; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Everything we said about the legislation of Bosnia-Herzegovina having been taken over also relates to the litigation law, and the only thing that was changed was the translation of the Yugoslav dinars into Croatian dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a decree on the implementation of the decree laws on the adoption of the Law on Administrative Disputes and so on. I just want to point to Article 3. It says here: "The Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, department in Mostar, shall be responsible for administrative disputes." Now, for those of us who are not familiar with the legal system, could you please explain Article 3 to us. Why was it necessary for the Supreme Court to handle administrative disputes? And I assume the reason that we have the department in Mostar is because, as you've indicated, the Sarajevo -- the Supreme Court in Sarajevo was blocked.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. As was the case with other decrees, this one, too, changes the Law on Administrative Disputes only to the extent necessary for that particular law to be applied. One of these areas was the impossibility for the appeals to reach the relevant court in Sarajevo, and you can see in Article 2 that the provisions not to be applied will be the ones referring to proceedings before the federal court; in other words, the court of the former Yugoslavia. In all its other provisions, the law remained the same and remained in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is another decree. This is on the Law on Executive Procedure implementing -- implemented as a republican law in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time of war or imminent threat of war. Again, as we've indicated before, we can see that it's grounded in the republican law, with the exception of Article 2 which amends the quoted fees. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a federal law on the enforcement procedure; and as we can see, the only intervention was in the conversion of sums from Yugoslav dinars into Croatian dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at 1D 00138.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This one is a decree to amend the Law on Court Duties. And again, if we just look through it, this basically, consistent with your previous answers, just sets out the monetary values. It changes to reflect the Croatian dinar as a result of the challenges as you've indicated before; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In contrast to the other decrees, this particular decree, due to a galloping inflation which completely devalued court fees, a more extensive intervention had to be made which went beyond the conversion of Yugoslav dinars to Croatian dinars; that's to say, the fees had to be raised to compensate for the devaluation of the currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 00139, 1D 00139.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a decree on the application on the rules of procedure of regular courts. And I just wish to point out a couple of things for your comment on, again very briefly. Article 5, we can see the dinars are being changed to reflect Croatian dinars; but Article 2, it says: "In the text of the Rules of Procedure of Regular Courts, the words 'Ministry of Justice and Administration' shall be replaced with the words 'Department of Justice and General Administration of the HZ HB ...'" Was there a reason for that change?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A specific reason was the fact that the republican Ministry of Justice was physically cut off and was not able to discharge its duties; and under Article 2, these duties were deferred to the department of justice and general administration. And as you rightly state, in Article 5, the amounts were converted into Croatian dinars. All the other provisions of the rules of procedure remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, again, I want to go back to the question that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: -- interrupt you, and we are now approaching the end of today's meeting. But anyway, I have of course listened carefully to your questions and the answers concerning the Croatian dinars issue, and somehow I am a bit perplexed since last time when Mr. Primorac was here, that time Mr. Primorac and the documents which you have submitted mainly wish to suggest and to demonstrate that actually it was not the Croatian dinars which had been mainly used. Now during the very last -- during the presentation of the last documents, I believe that, probably I am not wrong, when I say that here everywhere the Croatian dinars are being mentioned, like in one of the last documents, that is, 1D 00139, 00139. And then in that one, in that decree, Article 5, it says that: "In all provisions of Article 1 of the Rules, the word 'Croatian' shall be added before the word 'dinar.'" So my only question is that probably we should give some further attention to this issue as far as the use of the Croatian dinar is concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for that observation, Judge Prandler, and I can assure you - you may rest assured - that that issue will be dealt with when we have the head of the department of finance who will come here and he will explain to us why it was necessary. So I trust you can wait until the head of -- that will be in September. It's not too far off. But we will answer that question for you. I just wanted to, in the time that we have left, just ask one question that might go back to the question that was asked by Judge Trechsel with respect to "ministry" versus "department."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know terminologically speaking, terminologically speaking, in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a hierarchical sense, "ministry" versus "department," are they at the same level or is one above the other? And I'm saying that as a result of Article 2 in this particular decree, which is 1D 00139; and, again, this is a follow-up question from Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell, as a rule, departments are only portions of ministries, because in Bosnia-Herzegovina, ministries are composed of departments, which are in turn composed of several offices, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think that's it for the day. And I hope, Judge Trechsel, with that explanation, now you can rest assured that at least in Switzerland, we know that a department is the same as a ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Witness, you will return for the hearing tomorrow at 9.00, and Mr. Karnavas has one hour, 30 minutes left. Pleasant afternoon. See you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of July, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.
